detail_additions.text: New apple rootstocks are evaluated mainly through the multistate NC-140 research project, and growers should know each rootstock's capabilities and limitations. The guides' rootstock descriptions compare fruit size among rootstocks; for example, Vineland 1 gives fruit size equal to or greater than M.26.

detail_additions.text: For espalier, the fruiting habit of the cultivar matters. Spur-bearing fruit trees are easier to espalier because much new growth can be removed without losing productivity as long as the spurs stay intact, whereas tip-bearing trees, which fruit at or near the branch tips, are harder to train.

detail_additions.text: The USDA Plant Hardiness Zone Map is based on the average annual extreme minimum winter temperature, shown as 10 °F zones from zone 1 (coldest) to zone 13 (warmest), each split into 5 °F half zones 'a' and 'b'. A site's zone can be compared with a plant's hardiness rating; a plant rated hardy to a zone is expected to survive winter, with proper care, in that zone or a higher-numbered (warmer) one.

references.third_party_database: USDA ARS Plant Hardiness Zone Map: How to Use the Maps

detail_additions.text: Kaolinite-group minerals form mainly through hydrothermal alteration or weathering of feldspars under acid conditions and are used to make ceramics, paper and paint. Clay (kaolin) is a hydrated aluminium silicate sold as a white to yellowish or greyish fine powder (kaolinite, dickite and nacrite), and the US FDA affirms it as generally recognized as safe (GRAS) as an indirect human food ingredient under good manufacturing practice (21 CFR 186.1256).

detail_additions.text: Apple cultivars can differ in flowering date by more than 30 days. Trees are most sensitive to frost at full bloom, so late-flowering selections often escape freezing injury. Late bloom also means the trees flower later in spring, which matters when judging fire blight risk during bloom.

references.third_party_database: Mapping quantitative physiological traits in apple (Euphytica)

detail_additions.text: Apple union necrosis and decline is caused by tomato ringspot virus (TmRSV). The virus also causes disease in other fruit trees, such as Prunus stem pitting of peach and nectarine and brownline of Stanley prune, as well as in raspberry and many herbaceous plants, and the dagger nematode is its vector.

references.third_party_database: PNW Plant Disease Management Handbook

detail_additions.text: In whip-and-tongue bench grafting, the scion and rootstock are chosen to be the same diameter so that their cambial layers line up, which improves the chance that the graft takes.

references.third_party_database: Penn State Extension: Fruit Tree Propagation - Bench Grafting

detail_additions.item: Rootstock propagation and the nursery cycle
detail_additions.text: Apple is relatively hard to root from cuttings, so clonal rootstocks are propagated mainly by layering and the cultivar is then grafted or budded onto them. The traditional nursery tree takes three years: daughter liners are cut from the stool beds and graded in the first autumn, held in cold storage, lined out and budded, and the bud is grown on. Nurseries remove root suckers, which are rootstock genotype and unsuited to fruit production.

references.third_party_database: Cornell HORT 494: Propagation of clonal apple rootstocks

detail_additions.text: Cornell's table rates common cultivars not bred for scab resistance by scab susceptibility, from very susceptible (e.g. Ambrosia) through moderately susceptible (e.g. SunCrisp) to moderately resistant (e.g. Honeycrisp).

detail_additions.text: Drought stress in apple causes leaf wilting, yellowing and early leaf fall, and premature fruit ripening and drop. It also reduces leaf area and temporarily stops stem growth, and when drought coincides with heat, leaf scorching also occurs.

references.third_party_database: Horticulture Research (2023) review: apple responses to abiotic stress

detail_additions.text: Standard apple trees exceed 20 feet, semidwarf trees are usually 12–15 feet and dwarf trees 5–10 feet. MM.111, described as the most reliable semi-dwarf rootstock, gives large trees 16–20 feet tall that first crop at 5–7 years.

references.third_party_database: Oregon State University Extension EC 1622

detail_additions.text: Cropping is the best vigour control agent available for orchard crops: once a full canopy is established, fruit load diverts growth into fruit rather than wood and leaves, reducing tree size and vigour.

references.third_party_database: APAL: The Australian orchard of the future

detail_additions.text: The dwarfing effect of rootstocks differs from that of compact scions or chemical growth regulators. Growth retardants such as daminozide (Alar) act against gibberellin, which drives shoot extension and inhibits flower bud formation, and so shorten internodes and restrain tree size.

detail_additions.text: Apple has three periods of natural fruit drop, the first two of which may overlap. The first, 1–2 weeks after flowering, removes mostly abnormal and unpollinated flowers; the second, 4–6 weeks after bloom, is the heaviest and is known as June drop.

detail_additions.text: Skin colour often affects consumer preference and market acceptance of apples, and in general red apples are preferred.

references.third_party_database: Colorado State University Extension: Colorado Apples

detail_additions.text: Fruit is shed through an abscission zone of small, densely packed cells. Abscission has two processes that usually happen together: detachment of the fruit and formation of a protective layer, so the fruit is released without damage to the tree.

detail_additions.text: Cool (not necessarily freezing) weather and wet fruit, especially from pink until 3 weeks after petal fall, can cause russeting; Golden Delicious is most susceptible and markings are more abundant at the stem end. Russet develops from cracks in the fruit cuticle and injury occurs from the pink stage to about 40 days after petal fall.

detail_additions.text: Peel colour is one of the most important factors in market acceptance: red cultivars are generally preferred and, within a cultivar, more highly coloured fruit; preferences vary by country and region. Honeycrisp can bear both blushed fruit (never striped, even in less coloured areas) and striped fruit on the same tree and even the same spur, an unusual trait, whereas Royal Gala and Fireside stay striped and Connell Red, a sport of Fireside, stays blushed.

detail_additions.text: Sweetness, sourness, firmness and other sensory traits strongly influence consumer satisfaction. Sensory studies show that perceived sweetness and tartness do not always match measured sugar and acid content.

references.third_party_database: Mignard et al. (2022) Agronomy 12:827

detail_additions.text: Apples secrete their own natural wax, which is what shines when a picked apple is rubbed. Fresh fruit is 80–95% water and constantly loses moisture through respiration and transpiration; the wax protects apples against shrivelling and nutrient loss, helping them keep crispness and moisture.

references.third_party_database: USApple: Apples and Wax Backgrounder

detail_additions.text: Bitter pit spots are 0.125–0.25 inch across, normally develop after harvest and never approach the size of large cork spots; they start dark brown and quickly become blackish. These differences in appearance separate the two disorders, and both may be reduced by the nutrient sprays in the guide's orchard nutrition section.

detail_additions.text: Most apple varieties are self-incompatible and need cross-pollination from a compatible polliniser to set viable fruit, and polliniser identity affects fruit set. In Western Cape orchards without managed honeybees, wild honeybees provided this pollination as a free ecosystem service.

detail_additions.text: Thread blight, caused by Corticium stevensii, is mainly a problem of poorly managed southeastern US orchards; from early summer, leaves on interior or shaded branches wilt, brown and cling mid-branch, and diagnosis rests on the fungus: a white mycelial fan ahead of dead leaf tissue, fine threads tying leaves to petioles and twigs, and superficial silvery-tan rhizomorphs (to 1/16 inch) and sclerotia (to 3/16 by 1/8 inch) that scrape off bark and fruit without harming the wood. Sclerotia overwinter (eastern Kentucky), leaf blight appears in late spring on branches carrying them and spreads leaf to leaf, and disease is worse in moist, shaded sites; in well-managed orchards it is usually seen only after harvest, once fungicide sprays stop. Once established it is hard to control with fungicides, so rely on preventive sprays before infection, avoid hollows and other shaded, poorly ventilated sites, prune out blighted twigs under light pressure, and prune to let in sun and air.

references.third_party_database: WVU Kearneysville Fruit Pathology: Thread Blight

detail_additions.text: X-spot (also X-rot or Nigrospora spot) is a small, circular, depressed necrotic spot usually on the calyx end of fruit in the mid-Atlantic region; it is uncommon but reached 86% on unprotected Golden Delicious and Rome Beauty, and Jonathan, Stayman Winesap and York Imperial are also susceptible. A fungus is associated with the lesions, but the typical symptom has not been reproduced by inoculation and the disease cycle is unresolved. Fungicides applied for summer diseases give effective control.

references.third_party_database: WVU Kearneysville Fruit Pathology: X-spot

detail_additions.text: Windbreaks protect fruit trees and developing fruit from wind breakage in new orchards. Apple trees themselves are less wind tolerant than the species normally used in windbreaks.

references.third_party_database: OMAFRA: Using windbreaks in new orchards

detail_additions.text: Chemical thinners must diffuse across the cuticle covering leaves, flowers and young fruit, and waxes on the cuticle are a major barrier to penetration. In cold, cloudy weather little wax is secreted, so more chemical penetrates.
